era_visual_canon.clothing: Mine and mill workers: sweat-stained cotton work shirts or singlets, khaki shorts or drill trousers, leather work boots, wide-brimmed felt or slouch hats, usually no respirator or only a cloth rag over the face, clothing coated in pale fibrous dust. Prospectors of the late 1930s: rough flannel or cotton shirts, braces, heavy trousers, battered felt hats. Migrant wives and town women: light cotton shift or shirtwaist dresses, sandals, headscarves against the sun and dust. Children: cotton shorts and short-sleeved shirts or simple dresses, often barefoot in the dust. Company managers, inspectors and health officials: lightweight suits or short-sleeved shirts with ties, felt hats, polished shoes. Later decades: 1970s-1980s suits for lawyers and politicians; present-day Banjima community members and advocates in contemporary outdoor clothing, only in explicitly present-day scenes.
era_visual_canon.technology: Mid-century industrial and domestic technology: jaw crushers, mill machinery, belt conveyors, hessian bagging of fibre, hand tools and pneumatic rock drills, explosives for blasting. Valve radios, rotary-dial telephones, manual typewriters, carbon-copy reports, film cameras producing black-and-white and sepia prints, kerosene and early electric lighting, mechanical gauges. NO digital displays, NO LEDs, NO computers or mobile phones in mining-era scenes, NO modern dust-extraction or sealed respirators, NO hazmat suits before the late 20th century.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Late-1930s to 1960s utility trucks and flatbed tipper trucks hauling and dumping tailings, rugged four-wheel-drive utility vehicles, mill crushers and conveyors at the mine, small twin-engine propeller passenger aircraft landing on a dirt airstrip, ocean passenger liners for the migrant voyage from Europe via the Suez Canal. Later decades: 1970s-1980s four-wheel drives and sedans; demolition equipment in the 1986-1992 and 2022-2023 phases.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Small company houses built of timber, corrugated iron and fibro-cement sheeting, sparse mid-century furniture, louvred or fly-screened windows, dust settling on every surface; the mill interior choked with suspended dust; the town hospital with iron-frame beds and basic surgical equipment; the school, kindergarten and church on tailings-surfaced grounds; government offices with filing cabinets and typewriters; later courtrooms and parliamentary committee rooms; a 1980s airport passport-control desk.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: In historical scenes (1937-1992): no smartphones, no LED or flat-panel screens, no modern hi-vis vests, no sealed modern respirators or hazmat suits, no plastic safety barriers, no modern pickup trucks or SUVs, no paved asphalt roads in the town, no modern signage or branded logos, no contemporary clothing, no drones, no solar panels.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Houses and buildings of corrugated iron, timber and fibro-cement (asbestos-cement) sheeting; roads, yards, schoolyard, public spaces and the airstrip surfaced with crushed fibrous asbestos tailings; raw crocidolite fibre that frays and crumbles when handled, releasing a fine dust that coats everything; loose fine dust over bare desert earth and gorge rock.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: Intense red Pilbara earth and red dust surrounding the town, against blue-grey crocidolite tailings spread across roads, yards and the airstrip, with pale dust clouds hanging over the mill.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: Wittenoom Asbestos Management Area of 46,840 hectares; more than three million tonnes of tailings left behind; about 150,000 tonnes of commercial asbestos produced by three mines between 1937 and 1966; a small isolated town served by a short dirt airstrip for small propeller aircraft.
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: An isolated Pilbara mining town where the very ground — roads, yards, schoolyard and airstrip — was paved with blue crocidolite tailings set against intense red earth. Today it is a demolished, depopulated forbidden zone sealed by permanent barricades.
era_visual_canon.demographics: Mining-era population of Australian mine and mill workers with high turnover, European displaced persons assigned to work contracts (1948-1951), European recruits brought by CSR from 1950, and Spanish migrant families under the 1958 Spain-Australia agreement in the early 1960s, including wives and young children. Workers wore dust-coated work shirts, shorts and felt hats without respiratory protection. The surrounding land belongs to Banjima traditional owners, Aboriginal Australians documented in the 2020s legal action. Later, a dwindling handful of residents remained until 2022-2023.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: No sourced visual research block was provided. All place descriptions come from TEXT sources: oral testimony (red earth, dust everywhere, houses of corrugated iron, timber and fibro-cement; children handling asbestos), official reports (dust-covered mill, tailings on roads, yards and airstrip, water-borne deposits in creeks, permanent barricades) and press accounts. Family photographs are referenced in text but not supplied: a portrait with a bandaged foot, a baptism photo dated 7 July 1963, and sepia family photographs shown in an interview. No architectural plans, footage or archive images are in the pool. Colour of tailings is inferred from the mineral's common name (blue asbestos). Building dimensions are not documented; scale figures are area and tonnage only. Demographic ethnicity comes from written records, not photographs.

condition_evolution.at_event: Operating mining town in the early 1960s: a working mill shrouded in thick dust, small houses of corrugated iron, timber and fibro-cement, roads, yards, schoolyard and airstrip freshly surfaced with tailings delivered by company trucks, families and children living in the dust, small propeller planes landing on the dirt strip.
condition_evolution.later: From 1978 the state shrank the town; buildings were demolished and the school, nursing post and police station closed in 1986-1992; the airport closed in 1993; power was cut in 2006; the town was abolished and erased from maps and signs in 2006-2007; the last residents left in 2022-2023 with final demolition of structures; wind and water carry tailings into creeks, pools and floodplains toward the Fortescue River; permanent barricades now block every access.

periods.clothing: Prospectors and early miners in rough flannel or cotton shirts, heavy trousers with braces, felt hats and leather boots; officials and inspectors in three-piece suits and fedoras.
periods.technology: Hand tools, early pneumatic drills, blasting explosives, valve radios, telegraph and manual typewriters; no plastics, no electronics.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1930s-1940s utility trucks and small flatbed lorries on dirt tracks, rudimentary early mill machinery at Yampire and Wittenoom gorges.
periods.interiors: Rough timber and corrugated-iron huts and camp buildings, kerosene lamps, packed-earth floors, bare work benches.

periods.clothing: Miners and mill hands in singlets or cotton work shirts, khaki shorts, work boots and felt hats with no respirators, dust-covered; migrant women in light cotton dresses and headscarves; children in shorts or simple dresses, often barefoot; company managers and health officials in lightweight suits.
periods.technology: Full-scale mill with crushers, conveyors and fibre bagging, rudimentary dust-reduction equipment installed late, valve radios, rotary telephones, film cameras, typewritten reports and memos.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Tipper trucks delivering blue tailings to yards and roads, rugged four-wheel-drive utilities, small twin-engine propeller aircraft on the tailings airstrip, passenger liners carrying European migrants.
periods.interiors: Company houses of timber, corrugated iron and fibro-cement sheeting, the town hospital ward, school classrooms, dust-filled mill sheds.

periods.clothing: 1970s-1980s civilian clothing for remaining residents; suits and ties for lawyers, judges' robes in court, suits for parliamentarians and officials; former workers shown older in ordinary casual clothes.
periods.technology: CRT televisions, electric typewriters, photocopied legal documents, early office computers only from the late 1980s; airport passport desks with paper documents.
periods.vehicles_machinery: 1970s-1980s four-wheel drives and sedans, demolition machinery clearing town buildings in 1986-1992.
periods.interiors: Courtrooms, law offices, parliamentary committee rooms, a shrinking town with closed school, nursing post and police station.

periods.clothing: Present-day scenes only: Banjima traditional owners and advocates in contemporary outdoor clothing; government and legal figures in modern business attire; no people inside the forbidden zone except as implied past.
periods.technology: Contemporary technology permitted only in explicitly present-day segments (legal offices, interviews); the town itself shows no functioning infrastructure after the 2006 power disconnection.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Modern four-wheel drives outside the zone, demolition equipment in 2022-2023, permanent barricades across access roads.
periods.interiors: Interview settings with sepia family photographs, legal and government offices; the town has no surviving interiors after final demolition.

people_groups.who: Asbestos miners, mill hands, fitters and laborers at Wittenoom, a high-turnover mix of Australians and European migrants.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom mines and mill from 1937 to 1966, documented especially in 1946-1959 dust disputes and the 1957 Board of Reference inspection; survivors appear as aging former workers in the 1980s.
people_groups.appearance: Mixed Australian and European men, fair to olive skin with sun-darkened faces and arms, lean and muscular from heavy manual labor, skin, hair and clothes coated in fine pale fibrous dust.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Rough cotton or flannel work shirts, heavy trousers with braces, leather boots and battered felt hats, no respiratory protection.
Singlets or short-sleeved cotton work shirts, khaki shorts, work boots and felt or slouch hats, short practical haircuts, dust-caked clothing with at most a cloth rag over the mouth.
Aging former workers in ordinary 1980s casual shirts and trousers, some visibly frail from illness.

people_groups.who: Australian prospectors who opened the blue asbestos workings in the Hamersley Ranges and later held mine interests.
people_groups.where_when: Yampire and Wittenoom gorges from 1937 to 1943.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men with sun-weathered fair skin, wiry builds hardened by outback prospecting.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Rough flannel or cotton shirts with rolled sleeves, heavy work trousers, leather boots and wide-brimmed felt hats suited to desert heat.

people_groups.who: Postwar European displaced persons assigned by the federal government to work contracts in Wittenoom, followed by European recruits brought by CSR.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom from 1948 to 1951 for displaced persons, with European recruitment continuing from 1950 onward.
people_groups.appearance: European men of varied fair to light-olive complexion, lean postwar builds, sunburned under the Pilbara sun.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Simple cotton work shirts and trousers or shorts, work boots and felt hats on site; worn woollen jackets and caps from Europe on arrival.

people_groups.who: Spanish miners, their wives and young children who emigrated under the 1958 Spain-Australia migration agreement.
people_groups.where_when: Sea voyage from Málaga via Suez and arrival in Wittenoom in 1962, living there from 1962 to about 1964, returning to Madrid in 1966 and 1971; recalled in later interviews into the 2020s.
people_groups.appearance: Spanish Mediterranean features, light-olive to fair skin, dark brown or black hair, the men lean and strong from mine work, the women young, the children small and dust-covered.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Men in cotton work shirts, shorts, boots and felt hats with neatly combed short dark hair; women in light cotton dresses, sandals and headscarves with set or pinned-up hair; children in cotton shorts or simple dresses, often barefoot; Sunday best and white christening gown for the baptism.
Late-1960s Spanish urban clothing on return to Madrid: men in jackets and trousers, women in knee-length dresses and cardigans.
Grown children and aging parents in ordinary contemporary civilian clothing during airport, interview and remembrance scenes.

people_groups.who: Children raised in Wittenoom, including Spanish migrant children who played with raw asbestos and those born in the town hospital.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom streets, yards and schoolyard from 1962 to 1965.
people_groups.appearance: Young children of Australian and European, including Spanish, origin, fair to olive skin, dusty hair and limbs from playing on tailings.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Cotton shorts and short-sleeved shirts or simple cotton dresses, bare feet or sandals, short cropped or plaited hair, clothes dusted with fine fibre.

people_groups.who: Managers and executives of ABA and its parent company CSR, a former sugar-industry firm with little mining experience.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom mine offices and company headquarters from 1943 to 1966, including the 1949 employer hearings and the 1966 closure announcement.
people_groups.appearance: Australian businessmen of the period, fair-skinned, office-based builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Lightweight or dark business suits with ties, felt hats, polished shoes, short-back-and-sides haircuts; shirtsleeves and tie when on site in the heat.

people_groups.who: Mines inspectors, state mining engineers, public health doctors, health commissioners, an industrial hygienist, a prime minister, members of the Wittenoom Steering Committee and state government bodies.
people_groups.where_when: Inspections, reports and decisions on Wittenoom from 1944 to 1968, continuing through state government reduction of the town from 1978.
people_groups.appearance: Australian officials and doctors, mostly fair-skinned office professionals, middle-aged.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Suits or short-sleeved shirts with ties, felt hats, white coats for doctors, notebooks and clipboards during inspections.
1970s-1980s business suits with wider lapels and ties in government offices.

people_groups.who: Australian Workers' Union representatives and members of the labour arbitration bodies and Board of Reference who negotiated dust allowances.
people_groups.where_when: Award negotiations and hearings concerning Wittenoom from 1946 to 1959, including the 1957 mill inspection.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men, union officials with working-class builds and arbitration officials with office builds, fair to sun-darkened skin.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Union men in open-collar shirts and jackets or simple suits; arbitration members in formal suits and ties with hats.

people_groups.who: Western Australian parliamentary inquiry leaders, committee chairs, premiers and lands ministers dealing with clean-up recommendations.
people_groups.where_when: Western Australian parliament and government offices in 1992, 1994, 2016 and 2019.
people_groups.appearance: Australian politicians, predominantly middle-aged office professionals.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Early-1990s dark business suits with broad shoulders, patterned ties and conservative haircuts.
Contemporary tailored business suits, open-collar or tied shirts.

people_groups.who: Former workers, residents and families who formed the Asbestos Diseases Society of Australia, along with their lawyers and the society's leadership.
people_groups.where_when: Western Australia from 1979 through the 1988 verdict and 1989 settlement, continuing into the 2020s.
people_groups.appearance: Australian and European-origin men and women of varied ages, many former workers visibly aged or ill.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Ordinary 1980s civilian clothing for victims; lawyers in suits and ties, judges in court robes.
Contemporary professional attire for advocates and lawyers.

people_groups.who: Banjima Aboriginal traditional owners of the land around Wittenoom, including elders and BNTAC leadership pursuing remediation.
people_groups.where_when: Banjima country around Wittenoom in 2023-2026, including the UN rapporteur's 2023 visit, an elder's death in 2024, and the 2025-2026 legal action.
people_groups.appearance: Aboriginal Australian men and women with dark brown skin, dark hair often greying in elders, features typical of Pilbara Aboriginal people.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Contemporary outdoor clothing suited to Pilbara heat — cotton shirts, work trousers and broad-brimmed hats — or neat collared shirts for meetings and legal announcements.

people_groups.who: Australian airport police officer at passport control who recognized Wittenoom as a birthplace.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Mid-1980s Australian police uniform with pale-blue collared shirt, epaulettes and cap, seated at a passport desk.

people_groups.who: The few residents who remained in Wittenoom after its formal abolition.
people_groups.where_when: Wittenoom from 2006 until their departure or eviction in 2022-2023.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Practical contemporary outback clothing — work shirts, shorts or jeans, broad-brimmed hats and boots.
